analysis.one_liner: Requires upfront all-in ticket pricing, bans bot buying and fake ticket sites, and adds FTC penalties.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill requiring full upfront ticket pricing and tougher penalties for bot-driven ticket buying died in committee without a vote, with 12 cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 5 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fans First Act would have forced anyone selling event tickets to show the full price — face value plus every fee — from the first ad to checkout. It would ban resellers from selling tickets they don't actually have, ban websites that pretend to be official artist or venue sites, require refunds when events are canceled, and make ticketing companies build real defenses against automated bots that buy up tickets instantly. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could impose civil penalties, and a government study would examine how resellers get tickets and whether exclusive contracts between Ticketmaster and venues raise prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary fans buying concert, sports, and theater tickets. They would see the true total price before checkout instead of discovering large fees at the last screen, get refunds when events are canceled, be warned clearly when buying from a resale site rather than the official box office, and face better odds of buying at face value because bot attacks and speculative listings would carry civil penalties of at least $15,000 per day plus up to $10,000 per intentionally sold ticket [S2]. Artists, venues, and teams would also gain the right to stop resale sites from using their names and logos to look official [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Sellers must display the total event ticket price, itemizing face value, taxes, and every ancillary fee, in any ad or interface that shows a price and at every step of checkout [S2].
Resellers may not sell or advertise a ticket unless they have actual possession of it, ending 'speculative ticketing' where scalpers list tickets they do not yet hold [S2].
Resale sites may not use artist, venue, or team names, logos, or lookalike URLs to pose as official or endorsed, and must clearly disclose that they are not the primary seller [S2].

If an event is canceled, buyers get at minimum a full refund of the total ticket price plus taxes, unless the cancellation was caused by something beyond the organizer's control such as a natural disaster [S2].

The bill strengthens the 2016 BOTS Act: ticket issuers must enforce purchase limits with real security measures, report bot circumvention incidents to the FTC within 30 days, and the FTC gains civil action authority with penalties of at least $10,000 per day of violation plus $1,000 per violation, or $10,000 per violation if intentional [S2].

Violations of the new ticketing rules are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, with penalties of at least $15,000 per day, the greater of $1,000 per violating ticket or five times total ticket prices, and $10,000 per ticket for intentional violations; state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents for injunctions and restitution [S2].
A GAO study would examine how professional resellers obtain tickets, 'buy and hold' market manipulation, and whether exclusive contracts between primary sellers and venues harm the market [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Secondary ticketing platforms and professional brokers would bear the direct costs: penalties for fake 'official' marketing and speculative listings, mandatory disclosures, and lost revenue from practices the bill outlaws. Primary ticketing companies like Ticketmaster would pay to build and maintain anti-bot security systems and report incidents to the FTC. Some of those compliance costs could surface as slightly higher service fees, and the heaviest penalties on violators would come out of resale-industry profits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Resale platforms, brokers, and primary ticketing companies

drawbacks.text: The refund guarantee has a large carve-out: no refund is required when a cancellation stems from a cause beyond the organizer's reasonable control, such as a natural disaster or civil disturbance, so some canceled events would still leave buyers without their money [S2].

The bill regulates marketing and fraud but does not cap resale prices or ban the exclusive venue contracts that have made one company the dominant ticket seller; it only orders a government study of those exclusive contracts, so the underlying market structure fans complain about would remain [S2].

Heavy per-ticket and per-day penalties and mandatory security and reporting systems could raise compliance costs that ticketing companies pass along in fees, and the machinery largely relies on FTC enforcement capacity rather than giving fans a private right to sue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and targeted at practices fans actually experience — surprise fees, bot emptying of on-sales, counterfeit-looking resale sites, and no refunds after cancellations. The costs fall mostly on resale platforms and brokers, and compliance costs would likely be modest relative to the fees the industry already charges. The honest limitation is that the bill treats symptoms of a concentrated market without touching the exclusive contracts that create it, and its refund right weakens in exactly the messy-cancellation cases where fans need it most. On balance it is a well-aimed consumer bill with gaps.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2023 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. John Cornyn introduced the Fans First Act on December 7, 2023, joined by Sens. Klobuchar, Blackburn, Welch, Wicker, and Lujan as original cosponsors — three Republicans and three Democrats [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced [S1].
No committee vote, floor action, or further step followed; the complete action history ends with the referral to committee [S4].
The bill gathered 12 cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but that bipartisan support never converted into a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and any bill not passed dies with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Secondary ticketing platforms and professional resellers, which keep operating with hidden fees, speculative listings, and lookalike official sites, and primary ticketing companies face no new anti-bot security duties. Fans keep paying undisclosed fees at checkout and competing with bots for face-value tickets.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split — the six original sponsors were three Republicans and three Democrats, and the 12 additional cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 5 Republicans [S2][S3] — so the bill died without a vote for reasons other than partisan opposition.

industries.industry: Secondary ticketing exchanges (StubHub, SeatGeek, Vivid Seats and similar resale platforms)
industries.note: The bill bans speculative listings, outlaws using artist and venue names and lookalike URLs to appear official, requires prominent disclosure that a site is not the primary seller, and exposes exchanges to per-ticket and per-day civil penalties. Their profits depend on markup-driven resale and marketing that makes fans believe they are on an official site, which puts the industry's interest directly against the fans the bill protects.

Brokers could no longer sell or advertise tickets they do not possess, could not use fan-club presales freely, and the GAO would study how they acquire inventory, including 'buy and hold' tactics that inflate resale prices. The bill targets exactly the practices that let brokers take tickets ahead of ordinary buyers.

They gain from tougher anti-bot enforcement that protects on-sales from automated bulk buying, but they must build and maintain real access-control and security systems, report circumvention incidents to the FTC within 30 days, and face a GAO study of their exclusive venue contracts. They keep their dominant market position either way, since the bill studies but does not restrict exclusive contracts.

The bill makes it unlawful for resale sites to use their names, logos, or venue lookalikes without authorization, and gives them the option to receive resale buyers' contact information for safety and cancellation notices. Their interest runs alongside fans', since both are hurt by fake official-looking resale sites.
